Ah yes, sorry about that, I'm afraid this is a consequence of my PR being a bit of a hack! I think that either resource packs and filesystems need a larger overhaul so that the bug #90425 fixes can be resolved in a better way that doesn't require scanning the whole project, or maybe the process can be  optimized and sped up somehow on Android?

> or maybe the process can be optimized and sped up somehow on Android

Yeah, this seems to be particularly bad on Android. I don't know much about the Android side of things, but judging by the various system APIs in those call stacks it would seem that it's messing around with ZIP files a bunch, which seems somewhat inefficient.

Maybe there's some low-hanging fruit in terms of caching that could help improve things?
APK is a ZIP file, and Android do not extract it when installing, so some overhead is expected. But seems Android FS handler doing something wrong, `current_is_dir` should not iterate over all files.

```kt
		val fileName = ad.files[idx]
		// List the contents of $fileName. If it's a file, it will be empty, otherwise it'll be a
		// directory
		val filePath = if (ad.path == "") fileName else "${ad.path}/${fileName}"
		val fileContents = assetManager.list(filePath)
		return (fileContents?.size?: 0) > 0
```
Taking a full directory listing just to check if it's a directly doesn't look like a good idea.
Maybe @m4gr3d has some insight into whether `AssetsDirectoryAccess.kt` could be optimized a bit, or whether we do in fact need a more proper replacement solution for #90425 to fix this.

I don't think there's a better alternative.
`AssetManager` does not provide metadata to differentiate between files and directories, the only reliable way to check if a path is a directory is by using the current implementation.
The results of this check can be cached at least (and reused for other similar calls like `dir_exisst`).

> I don't think there's a better alternative.

Also, what about trying to open it as a file for reading and checking if it fails, this might be faster.

> > I don't think there's a better alternative.
> 
> Also, what about trying to open it as a file for reading and checking if it fails, this might be faster.

It might be slightly faster but would be unreliable. If opening a file fails, it could also mean the path simply doesn’t exist.


> The results of this check can be cached at least (and reused for other similar calls like dir_exisst).

Caching sounds good to me. We can definitely cache if a path is a directory or a file.

Would caching really help in this issue? The method would still do the same thing for each new path, and caching would introduce an additional lookup to check if the path is already cached. It would be only helpful if same path is checked again.

Another option, stop using `AssetManager` for directory listings at all, we know list of files at export, so we can save PCK header/index and use it. Reading actual file contents will use `AssetManager`, but all directory operations will use the same code as PCK and data fully loaded to memory, like it is done on other platforms.

> Another option, stop using `AssetManager` for directory listings at all, we know list of files at export, so we can save PCK header/index and use it. Reading actual file contents will use `AssetManager`, but all directory operations will use the same code as PCK and data fully loaded to memory, like it is done on other platforms.

Okay, something like this:

1. Generate a file at export time. It would be a single-level dictionary where:
    - Keys = Full asset paths
    - Values = true (directory) or false (file)
2. Load it into memory at startup.
3. Use it for all directory-related checks.

> Would caching really help in this issue? The method would still do the same thing for each new path, and caching would introduce an additional lookup to check if the path is already cached. It would be only helpful if same path is checked again.

I gave caching (on the Kotlin side) a quick try, just to check, and it does seem to have a significant effect, taking the repro down from about 24 seconds to 13 seconds on my device.

Still pretty costly though, so I would imagine storing the directory listing at export is the better alternative.

Caching at export also doesn’t seem to be an optimal approach here. The number of cached files is too large, causing excessive memory usage and repro project crashing due to an out-of-memory error during app startup.

I wouldn't say my method for saving/loading the cache file was perfect—it could crash due to flaws in my logic 😅. Someone else might want to give it a try and could potentially make this approach work.

> The number of cached files is too large, causing excessive memory usage and repro project crashing due to an out-of-memory error during loading.

How this is possible? Even the full PCK header/index with all file metadata for these 5000 files should be ~less than 500KiB~ *(about 1MB, since there's remap file for each scene)*, that's nothing in the terms of memory.

I would probably do it by reusing most of the PCK handling code instead of make an Android specific cache. This might also fix other APK related issues, like https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/103046, since file access will be more consistent with other platforms.

Basically add a "sparse bundle mode" flag to the headed, and change these lines to read separate files instead of the single PCK if it's set, and export PCK as on other platforms, but actual file content is written to a separate files instead of PCK:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/70eb62faf24223f1dcf90589f4b39d1be7609ca0/core/io/file_access_pack.cpp#L469-L474

I'll check it later, we probably do not want big changes like this for 4.4 at this stage.

A quick test of my idea (without any Android relates stuff for now) - https://github.com/bruvzg/godot/commit/99670d600f834b536f10dc00241159c84260fee4 PCK metadata is saved as with normal PCK, but files saved separately, all of this can be store in the APK. All directory handling is done by `FileAccessPack` as if it was PCK, but file contents access still handled by platform specific `FileAccess`.
